rv.q: Its current revival, directed by Lear deBessonet as part of Parks's retrospective residency at the Signature, is devastating.
Besides Jah, who imbues her character with a sensitive balance of pathos and dignity, the production benefits from an excellent ensemble...
Her name was Saartjie (Sarah) Baartman, but in the years of her fame she was called the “Venus Hottentot,” much like Joseph Merrick who, some decades later, would become famous as the “Elephant Man.”

Yet Ms. deBessonet’s production as a whole never achieves a compelling unity of vision, or the hypnotic flow of Signature’s recent revival of another early play by Ms. Parks, “The Death of the Last Black Man in the Whole Entire World.”
Balancing pathos, power and enthusiastic sensuality, Zainab Jah shows us the complex woman behind the stage figure that fascinates white customers with her 'primitive' abandon.

"'Venus' is pageant-like, intellectual and reminiscent of 'The Elephant Man.' And now Lear deBessonet has staged an excellent revival of the play...Whether the play’s bold and self-aware theatricality adds to or detracts from the impact of the storytelling is up for debate.
Venus is revealed as an intriguing and arresting work.
The script flows with poetry, music and moments that pop, like when the dexterous Zainab Jah slips into character as Venus.
Jah is superb at maneuvering the intricacies of such a complicated character.
Most importantly, one can leave the theater arguing just how much Baartman is truly a victim or a semi-willing party to her own demise.
Jah is marvelous here as a woman imprisoned, yet not wholly a victim.

"The play does a good job of bringing Saartjie's story to the fore. But over the course of the evening, things become less coherent...'Venus' has much of significance to say about the treatment of women and blacks.
As drama, Venus is less successful — because its steady fixation on Baartman's sexual objectification becomes repetitive over the course of two hours.
Venus comes across as both overelaborate and undercooked, a series of mirthless cartoons that state and restate its theme to diminishing effect.
Suzan-Lori Parks' extraordinary talents for once failed her.

In this dazzling production, Parks and deBessonet transform the stage into the Georgian era, boldly taking hold of the historical narrative and refusing to cede it back, giving Baartman's life the sympathetic perspective she richly deserves.
But in the end, Venus is a unique creation by a unique playwright with an urgent voice.
Each performance is finely tuned, and the direction of Lear DeBessonet brings the entire production to full throttled life.
Jah gives a spectacularly humanistic portrayal of a woman who is passed from man to woman to man as an object of spectacle, desire, and, ultimately, science.

It is a rich performance marked by an inscrutable coyness: 'I tell them what they want to hear,' she says in an aside, and we are left wondering how much she is referring to the other characters and how much she is referring to us.
Zainab Jah is prolific as Venus. She shows us her Venus layer by layer, as she is stripped and pawed.
Parks and deBessonet get to the heart of the matter early on; the bulk of the two-hour and fifteen-minute protest play merely hammers home the same ideas about gender, race, and cruelty.
As a play, Venus, now being revived at the Pershing Square Signature Theatre, is overlong (nearly two and a quarter hours) and frequently lifeless.
